issues.legal_issue: The presumption arising from a registered document recording an adoption is rebuttable.
material_facts: A registered adoption deed recording the adoption was produced in the dispute over the deceased’s estate.
The deed was signed by the person giving the child and the person taking the child in adoption.
issues.conclusion: The statutory presumption that the adoption complied with the law is rebuttable and does not make the registered deed conclusive.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, directs the court to presume compliance when a registered document purporting to record an adoption is produced and signed by the giver and taker, but the words “unless and until it is disproved” make the presumption rebuttable. The Court concurred with Modan Singh v. Mst. Sham Kaur & Ors. (AIR 1973 P&H 122).

predicates.adoption_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a claimed adoption was made in compliance with the law.
predicates.registered_adoption_document_signed_by_g: The person giving the child and the person taking the child signed a registered document purporting to record the adoption.

issues.definition: When an adoption dispute involves a registered adoption document signed by the giver and taker, compliance is presumed but may be disproved.

issues.legal_issue: Evidence contradicting a claimed adoption may rebut the presumption arising from its registered deed and support rejection of the adoption claim.
material_facts: A voters list prepared before the dispute identified the claimant as the son of his natural father, and he had also described himself that way in proceedings brought by his wife.
The deed recited that the child had been given and taken in adoption earlier, but no specific ceremonies or evidence of that giving and taking were produced.
Several records relied on to support the adoption were created after the suit began; the mutation proceedings occurred without notice, and related records were considered unreliable.
The deed and the later will contained circumstances that the lower courts considered suspicious.
issues.conclusion: The evidence was capable of rebutting the presumption; the concurrent rejection of the adoption claim was not shown to be perverse and was left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 16 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, contrary evidence may disprove the presumption created by a registered adoption document. Section 11(vi) requires the child to be actually given and taken in adoption with intent to transfer the child from the birth family to the adoptive family. The Court found that the evidence relied on by the lower courts could be considered in assessing whether the presumption had been rebutted.

rule.if: adoption_dispute and registered_adoption_document_signed_by_giver_and_taker and prior_records_identify_birth_father and adoption_giving_and_taking_lacks_support and post_dispute_supporting_records_are_unreliable

predicates.adoption_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a claimed adoption was made in compliance with the law.
predicates.registered_adoption_document_signed_by_g: The person giving the child and the person taking the child signed a registered document purporting to record the adoption.
predicates.prior_records_identify_birth_father: Records created before the dispute, or statements made independently of the adoption claim, identify the claimant as the child of the natural father.
predicates.adoption_giving_and_taking_lacks_support: The claimed act of giving and taking the child in adoption is not supported by evidence of the relevant event or ceremony.
predicates.post_dispute_supporting_records_are_unre: Records relied on to support the adoption were created after the dispute began or arose from proceedings lacking notice to affected persons.

issues.definition: In an adoption dispute, a registered deed does not prevent rejection of the adoption claim where prior records contradict it, the giving and taking lacks support, and later supporting records are unreliable.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court should not reappraise concurrent factual findings absent exceptional circumstances such as extreme perversity.
material_facts: The trial court rejected the adoption claim, and the first appellate court and High Court left that finding undisturbed.
The Supreme Court found that the evidence had been assessed by the lower courts and that their conclusion was not totally perverse.
The appeal sought further scrutiny of the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to reappraise the evidence or interfere with the concurrent findings, and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, scrutiny of evidence is not wholly prohibited, but interference with factual findings is reserved for exceptional cases involving extreme or total perversity; it is a rarity, not a regular practice. The Court expressed no opinion on Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_concurrent_fin: The proceeding is a special leave appeal from factual findings maintained by the lower courts.
predicates.evidence_reappraisal_is_sought: A party asks the reviewing court to scrutinize or reassess the evidence underlying those findings.
predicates.findings_are_not_perverse: The lower courts’ findings are not shown to be totally or extremely perverse.

issues.definition: In a special leave appeal seeking reappraisal of evidence, the Supreme Court leaves concurrent factual findings undisturbed when they are not perverse.
